implement: legion-worker: the implementer opens the pull request, writes its body from the template, pushes before completing and never waits on CI; this change's proof is an image-tag Job and three runner commands, all of which go in the body's E2E line and the handoff's proof array in that skill's six-field shape.

ce-simplify-code: the simplify pass is the implementer's, once per pull request, in its first implementing round; this change touches one Dockerfile RUN, one capability list and four documentation sites, which is exactly the shape that accumulates near-duplicate prose.
legion-retro: the same agent runs retro before the merger, writes any learning under docs/solutions/ and removes .legion/INFRA-221/ from the head that merges.
dispatch-first and dispatch: the implementer searches Dispatch before filing anything and opens a dispatch ask rather than an issue for any finding outside INFRA-221.
test: legion-worker: the tester drives the application rather than re-running CI, and must re-run the two surfaces this plan names — a Job in its own namespace on the pull request's image tag, and the three runner commands in its own container — then record implementerProof, failures and its own proof.
dispatch-first and dispatch: the same rule for anything the tester finds outside this issue.
review: legion-worker: the review round's order, the review of the head the handoff push made, and the review-threads discipline.

thermonuclear-deep-review: the correctness and security rubric, which matters here because the change adds five Debian packages to an image every agent of every project runs, and because one of them brings a client that reads a password from its environment.
thermonuclear-code-quality: the maintainability rubric over a diff whose risk is duplicated prose in six hand-maintained lists.

findings.finding: F1: 'in one documented step, without a person' is unmet by a plan whose halves all land in the worker image, since the image and the skills inside it reach a role only after someone pins a new digest; only the three ecosystem runners are true at today's digest.
findings.answer: Put to the architect, which answered on 2026-10-24: 'without a person' is about the step the role takes, not the deployment's roll, since every Legion change including the skills reaches a role through a digest roll. The plan carries both halves and names the roll as the known gap in its last section, as the parent issue named its own person-applied half.

findings.finding: F2: the file set for an apt-line change and a toolchain-name change is larger than the outline named, and docs/solutions/legion/find-every-copy-of-a-hand-maintained-list-by-its-last-member-alone-not-by-a-phrase-LEGION-764.md says to find the copies by the list's last member rather than by a phrase, and to grep twice.
findings.answer: The plan names every copy found by that grep (the Dockerfile's apt line, its justification comment, its header enumeration, the notices sentence, the toolchain smoke step and the final step's comment; four sites in docs/kubernetes.md; the published site's summary sentence; capabilities.go, image.go, capabilitiestest.go and the two expected-detail tests) and prescribes re-running the grep after implementing. The plan reviewer reproduced the grep and found no further copy.

findings.finding: F3: the spec's premise that INFRA-71 is 'through test and review with its section frozen' is contradicted by sjawhar/legion#2092, which is OPEN with CHANGES_REQUESTED, whose newest blocking finding is this issue's own subject, and which touches four of the same files.
findings.answer: Put to the architect, which answered: branch from main now, do not wait, forward-merge when #2092 lands, and quote the merged text as it ends up rather than as it reads today. The plan's ordering section records that, and records that restoring a psql example to the parent's section is a one-line edit in this pull request once the tool exists.

findings.finding: F4: none of the four 'what has to be true at the end' lines is machine-checkable as written, and a check for 'on PATH' must come from a child process rather than the harness's own shell.
findings.answer: The plan's acceptance table gives each line a surface, a command and a negative control, and uses bash -c 'type -P ...' for the on-PATH check. The image's /bin/sh is dash, whose type builtin has no -P, which the planner's rehearsal of the proof surface confirmed; the plan says so.

findings.finding: F5: extending the existing toolchain capability row versus adding a new row has an asymmetric cost the outline did not name.
findings.answer: The plan extends the existing row and states the measured reason: a row renders as name, status and detail with no tool list, so no contract type, no daemon API golden fixture and no end-to-end script changes, while a new row would touch at least seven further files.

findings.finding: F6: the proof surface was unmeasured in three links — whether the namespace can pull the image at all, whether its deadlines fit a 1 GiB cold pull, and the exact shape of the published tag, which is sha- plus twelve hex characters rather than a short sha.
findings.answer: Rehearsed end to end from this role container while planning: a Job on the currently pinned image was admitted, scheduled onto a machine created for it, pulled the image, ran, and its log was read back and the Job removed, 2 minutes 41 seconds from submission to Completed. The plan records the three things that rehearsal fixed, including the compute class the admission policy names and the deadline that fits the pull, and the tag's twelve-character shape from the workflow itself.

findings.finding: F7: the image cost was quoted as download size while this repository measures image cost as compressed image size.
findings.answer: The plan states both units and requires the written decision to carry the compressed size of the image this pull request builds beside the current pinned image's 1,018 MiB, each from its own manifest.

findings.finding: F8: a cached image layer's output is in the run that built it, so a second push leaves the apt step CACHED and its output in an earlier run.
findings.answer: An evidence rule in the plan's proof section: cite both run ids, and count the Setting up lines per stage, since a build stage installing the same package prints them too and never reaches the runtime image.

findings.finding: F9: three things the measurements did not settle — which tools (a product question), whether the spec's rejection of the per-issue install follows from its own number, and runtime.kubernetes.setup as a fourth option the spec does not list.
findings.answer: The tool list went to the architect and was confirmed with its reasons, MySQL excluded. The spec's number was wrong and the architect corrected the spec itself on being told. runtime.kubernetes.setup is recorded in the plan's decision table as rejected, with the history that makes it tempting.

findings.finding: F10: the line between 'installs into the pod' (the withheld operator-setup capability) and 'fetches onto the issue's checkout' is stated nowhere operationally, and one of the planner's own measurements sits on the forbidden side.
findings.answer: The plan draws the line by where the thing lands: under the container's own filesystem, bounded by the role's ephemeral limit and dying with the pod, versus under the issue's disk, which outlives the pod and is shared by the issue's roles. The .deb extraction is recorded in the decision table as rejected for being operator-setup under any reading, with the psql Perl-wrapper evidence that it is also fragile, so the next reader does not reach for it.

findings.finding: F11: a new legion-worker reference has its own guard tests, and legion-worker is not the skill an architect reads, so on the outline an architect would have no documented step and nothing in the checkout would carry one.
findings.answer: The plan puts the reference under skills/legion-worker/references/ with its row in that skill's References table and the skill:// link form the guard requires, adds one pointer in the architect's own skill, and adds a row to this repository's AGENTS.md WHERE TO LOOK table, which is the only home that reaches a role before the new image rolls.

findings.finding: F12: the proof is driven with an identity, a namespace, a compute class and a node pool belonging to the private deployment, and this repository is public; the parent's pull request is blocked on exactly that defect in its own plan file.
findings.answer: No such name appears in this plan, this handoff, any commit message of this generation or the planner's Dispatch writes. Every command reads the namespace from the projected token file instead, and the plan states the rule for the implementer and tester.

findings.finding: F13: 'never resolves something other than what was asked for' has no enforcement left, since the guard that would cover arbitrary commands is closed as not wanted.
findings.answer: The plan says so in its own section: no guard, no lint, no check that refuses, and the honest consequence that nothing stops a role typing a bare bunx name. What is delivered is a correct documented form and a present tool, proven by the pinned-versus-bare pair printing 2.6.3 against 0.3.3.

specDepartures.spec: The third candidate the spec prices is 'a runner the image provides that resolves a named, pinned tool and fails closed when it cannot', phrased as a mechanism the deployment would pay for and therefore build.
specDepartures.plan: No runner is built. The image already provides three, and the deliverable is the pinned form of each, documented where a role reads it, with its measured cost and its refusal.
specDepartures.evidence: Run in this role container on 2026-10-24: uvx ruff@0.14.0 --version is 1.12 s cold and 0.11 s warm; bunx --package @biomejs/biome@2.6.3 biome --version is 1.38 s; go run github.com/nats-io/natscli/nats@v0.1.5 --version is 103 s cold. Each refuses a version that does not exist and names it. A fourth wrapper would be machinery to maintain around three working commands.
